chapter.title: The model only talks. The agent does things.

cards.body:
Picture a new intern at the next desk. Ask them a question and they answer, then go back to scrolling their phone. That's a *chatbot*: a program that writes a reply and stops.

Now hand the same intern a task: 'get us a table for 7 tonight.' They stand up, make a call, hear 7 is full, take 7:30, and come back to tell you. **An agent is the intern who gets up from the desk.**
cards.simpler:
Think of a new helper sitting at the next desk. You ask a question, they answer, then they stop. That is a chatbot. It writes a reply and nothing else happens.

Now give that helper a job: 'get us a table for 7 tonight.' They get up, call the restaurant, hear 7 is full, take 7:30, and come back to tell you. **An agent is the helper who gets up and does the job.**

cards.prompt: You text your friend Priya twice. First: 'any good ramen near me?' She replies with a name. Then: 'book us a table for 7.' She calls, hears 7 is full, books 7:30, and texts you the confirmation. Which message turned Priya into an agent?

options.text: The first one. She used her knowledge to answer.
The second one. She took steps in the world and adjusted until the task was done.
Neither. Priya is a person, so the word doesn't apply.

whyNot.a: That's the chatbot move, not the agent move: she answered with words and stopped. Nothing in the world changed.
whyNot.c: That's the wrong test: the word is about what happens (steps toward a goal until done), not about who or what is doing it.

cards.reteach: The test is not how clever the reply is. It's whether something gets done after the reply. Answering 'any ramen?' changes nothing. Booking the table makes calls, hits a snag, adapts, and finishes. The second message set off a chain of actions. That chain is the agent.

cards.title: A chatbot writes and stops
cards.body:
Inside every chatbot is a *model*, the part that reads text and produces text. You type, it writes, it stops. That is the whole event. Even a brilliant answer is still just words on your screen.

The model cannot click, search, send, or pay. If it says 'I checked the website', it did not. It has no hands.

**An agent is the same model, given hands and a goal.** Code around the model lets it ask for an action, runs that action, and shows the model what happened. Then the model picks the next step, and the next, until it decides the goal is met.
cards.simpler:
Every chatbot has a model inside. It reads words and writes words. You type, it answers, it stops.

It cannot click, search, send, or pay. If it says 'I checked the website', it did not. It has no hands.

**An agent is the same model, given hands and a goal.** Extra code lets the model ask for an action, does it, and shows the model what happened. Then the model picks the next step until the job is done.

cards.title: Lisbon, Friday, two very different afternoons
cards.body:
Ask a chatbot for the cheapest flight to Lisbon on Friday. It writes a confident paragraph with an airline and a price. The price is a guess, because it never looked. You nod and move on.

Hand the same request to an agent. It searches a flight site, reads the results, picks a 6:40am departure, and tries to pay. The card is declined, so it stops and asks you. **Four actions, and one of them touched your money.** Same model underneath. Not the same afternoon.
cards.simpler:
Ask a chatbot for the cheapest flight to Lisbon on Friday. It writes a confident answer with an airline and a price. The price is a guess, because it never looked.

Give the same request to an agent. It searches a flight site, reads the results, picks a 6:40am flight, and tries to pay. The card fails, so it stops and asks you. **Four actions, and one of them touched your money.** Same model underneath. Not the same afternoon.

cards.prompt: Three things you could ask an AI tonight. Which one needs an agent, not a chatbot?

options.text: Paste in a rude email and ask for a polite reply you can copy.
Say 'clear the newsletters out of my inbox', and have it read the inbox, unsubscribe from 9 senders, archive 40 emails, and report back.
Ask what day of the week 14 March 2026 was.

whyNot.a: That's a chatbot job: one reply, and you do the sending. The only output is text.
whyNot.c: That's a one-shot answer, not a chain of steps. The model writes a word and stops.

cards.reteach: Ask: does the task end when the reply ends? A polite email and a day of the week both end as text on screen. Clearing an inbox means reading, deciding, clicking unsubscribe, archiving, and checking whether it's done yet. Many steps, each changing the real inbox. That's the agent.

cards.title: Why the difference changes everything
cards.body:
A chatbot's worst mistake is a wrong sentence. You read it, frown, and ignore it. Nothing happened.

An agent's worst mistake has already happened by the time you see it. The email went out. The file is gone. The ticket is bought for the wrong Friday.

**The agent is more useful and more dangerous for the exact same reason: it acts.** A chatbot needs you for every step. An agent does the boring middle on its own. That is the trade, and it is why the rest of this handbook is about what the intern may touch and who checks their work.
cards.simpler:
A chatbot's worst mistake is a wrong sentence. You just ignore it. Nothing happened.

An agent's worst mistake has already happened when you see it. The email went out. The ticket is for the wrong Friday.

**The agent is more useful and more dangerous for the same reason: it acts.** A chatbot needs you for every step. An agent does the dull middle alone. It is why the rest of this handbook asks what the helper may touch and who checks its work.

cards.body:
Dev asked a chatbot to cancel his gym membership. It replied, warmly, 'Done, I've cancelled it for you.' Three months of fees later, he learned it had no way to touch the gym's website. It had written the sentence a helpful person would write.

Spot it by asking one question: **what did it actually touch?** If the only thing that came out was words, it's a chatbot, however confident the words sound.
cards.simpler:
Dev asked a chatbot to cancel his gym membership. It replied warmly, 'Done, I've cancelled it for you.' Three months of fees later, he found out it had no way to reach the gym's website. It had just written the sentence a helpful person would write.

Spot this by asking one question: **what did it actually touch?** If all that came out was words, it is a chatbot, however sure the words sound.

cards.prompt: Your cousin asks: 'so what makes something an agent instead of a chatbot?' Which answer is the one from this chapter?

options.text: How smart the model is. Agents use bigger, better models.
Whether it takes real steps toward a goal and keeps going until the goal is done, instead of writing one reply and stopping.
Whether it remembers you from last time.

whyNot.a: That's the model, not the agent: the Lisbon example used the same model both times. The difference was the hands, not the brain.
whyNot.c: That's memory, which is a different idea (chapter 4). Your intern forgets everything overnight and is still an agent while on the task.

cards.reteach: Strip it to the simplest version. Chatbot: reply, stop. Agent: goal, step, look at what happened, next step, until done. Same model can sit inside either. What changes is whether the thing can act on the world and loop.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A chatbot is a model that writes a reply and stops; an agent is the same model given a goal and the ability to act, so it keeps taking steps until the job is done. **That one difference is why agents are both more useful and more risky**, and why what they may touch matters so much.
cards.simpler: A chatbot is a model that writes a reply and stops. An agent is the same model given a goal and the power to act, so it keeps taking steps until the job is done. **That one difference is why agents are both more useful and more risky.** It is also why what they may touch matters so much.

cards.body: Open ChatGPT or Claude and ask it to do something it has no way to do, like 'cancel my phone contract.' Watch whether it says it did it, or admits it can only write. Now you know which one you're talking to.
cards.simpler: Open ChatGPT or Claude and ask it to do something it has no way to do, like 'cancel my phone contract.' Then watch closely. Does it say it did it, or does it admit it can only write words? **Now you know which one you are talking to.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain to a friend, in 2 sentences, why asking ChatGPT a question is not an agent and why booking a flight with it would be.
